frictionVectors.title: European energy dependence
frictionVectors.details: Algeria retains strong bargaining power through pipeline gas and LNG, but European buyers are pursuing diversification and tighter contract flexibility. This limits Algiers' ability to convert energy access into sustained strategic concessions.

frictionVectors.title: Sahel and Western Sahara exposure
frictionVectors.details: Instability across the Sahel and tensions with Morocco continue to pressure Algeria's border security and regional diplomacy. External security partnerships remain sensitive because Algiers seeks to preserve strategic autonomy.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign control of hydrocarbons
frictionVectors.details: Angola is rebuilding production and negotiating investment while remaining dependent on foreign technology, capital, and operators in its offshore oil sector. Declining output and debt obligations constrain the state's room to capture greater value.

frictionVectors.title: Lobito corridor competition
frictionVectors.details: The corridor is drawing US, European, and Chinese attention because of its route toward copper and cobalt resources in the central African interior. Angola gains infrastructure and diplomatic leverage, but faces pressure over concession access, standards, and security.

frictionVectors.title: Port and logistics dependence
frictionVectors.details: Cotonou remains central to Benin's trade and fiscal model, leaving the country exposed to regional customs decisions and competition from Lagos and Lomé. Foreign-backed infrastructure improves capacity but can deepen dependence on external finance and operators.

frictionVectors.title: Sahel spillover
frictionVectors.details: Militant activity near the northern borders is increasing the cost of securing transport routes and rural communities. Benin is expanding security cooperation, but reliance on external training, equipment, and intelligence creates sovereignty trade-offs.

frictionVectors.title: Diamond market exposure
frictionVectors.details: Botswana has strengthened its negotiating position with major diamond partners and seeks more domestic sorting, trading, and beneficiation. However, weak global diamond demand and concentration in a few external buyers still limit sovereign leverage.

frictionVectors.title: Infrastructure and minerals race
frictionVectors.details: New interest in copper, coal, and other minerals could broaden the economy beyond diamonds, but transport and power constraints encourage reliance on foreign capital. The government is balancing investment access against strict environmental and revenue expectations.

frictionVectors.title: Gold-sector nationalization pressure
frictionVectors.details: The junta is seeking greater state control over gold production, refining, and marketing while confronting smuggling and opaque artisanal networks. Foreign firms remain important for capital and expertise, creating tension between revenue sovereignty and production needs.

frictionVectors.title: Russian security dependence
frictionVectors.details: The breakdown of defense ties with France and other Western partners has pushed Burkina Faso toward Russian security cooperation and regional junta coordination. This may increase short-term regime protection while deepening diplomatic isolation and concerns over external access to resources.

frictionVectors.title: Opaque Mining Partnerships
frictionVectors.details: Gold and 3TG mining remain vulnerable to informal exports, weak oversight, and opaque foreign-linked concessions. Limited state capacity reduces Burundi's ability to capture full value from its mineral base.

frictionVectors.title: Rwanda-DRC Security Spillover
frictionVectors.details: Tensions involving Rwanda, eastern DRC armed groups, and border security constrain trade corridors and increase military dependence. Instability also raises risks around mineral transit and regional infrastructure.

frictionVectors.title: External Dependence in Strategic Infrastructure
frictionVectors.details: Ports, airports, telecommunications, and energy systems rely heavily on European, Chinese, and multilateral financing. This improves connectivity but limits policy autonomy when debt, concessions, or operating contracts are renegotiated.

frictionVectors.title: Maritime Resource Protection
frictionVectors.details: Illegal fishing and narcotics trafficking challenge Cabo Verde's control over its large Atlantic maritime zone. Limited patrol capacity leaves enforcement dependent on European and wider international security partnerships.

frictionVectors.title: Chinese Infrastructure Leverage
frictionVectors.details: Chinese-financed roads, rail links, and port projects strengthen Cameroon’s logistics position but can create repayment, procurement, and concessionary leverage. The state remains exposed to external control of key trade infrastructure.

frictionVectors.title: Anglophone and Far North Insecurity
frictionVectors.details: Separatist conflict in the Northwest and Southwest and jihadist violence near the Lake Chad basin divert resources from national development. Insecurity disrupts transport, agricultural production, and access to extractive zones.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign Security Concessions
frictionVectors.details: Russian security personnel and affiliated commercial networks retain significant influence over regime protection and mining access. The arrangement strengthens short-term regime survival while weakening transparent sovereign control over gold and diamonds.

frictionVectors.title: Armed-Group Control of Corridors
frictionVectors.details: Armed groups and cross-border networks continue to contest roads, mining areas, and customs points. Dependence on foreign security providers and humanitarian logistics limits the government's independent control of national infrastructure.

frictionVectors.title: Pipeline and Oil Revenue Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Chad's oil sector remains tied to external operators and the Cameroon export corridor, limiting domestic leverage over pricing, transport, and revenue capture. Production volatility and weak transparency make fiscal sovereignty fragile.

frictionVectors.title: Sudan War Spillover
frictionVectors.details: The Sudan conflict has driven refugee flows, cross-border arms trafficking, and pressure on eastern Chad's security apparatus. Humanitarian and military dependence on outside partners is increasing as border management absorbs national resources.

highlights: External aid and remittances sustain resilience

frictionVectors.title: France and Mayotte
frictionVectors.details: France retains control of Mayotte, limiting Comoros's territorial sovereignty and fueling recurring diplomatic tension. Migration controls and maritime disputes periodically intensify friction.

frictionVectors.title: Aid and infrastructure dependence
frictionVectors.details: Transport, energy, and telecommunications projects remain heavily dependent on foreign financing and contractors, constraining domestic policy autonomy.

highlights: Critical minerals attract competing external powers

frictionVectors.title: Mineral competition and opaque supply chains
frictionVectors.details: Cobalt, copper, coltan, and gold continue to draw intense foreign commercial and strategic interest. Weak oversight and informal networks limit the state's ability to capture value and enforce traceability.

frictionVectors.title: Regional proxy conflict
frictionVectors.details: Armed groups and cross-border support networks in the east challenge Kinshasa's territorial authority. Security partnerships and diplomatic pressure from neighboring states remain essential but politically sensitive.

frictionVectors.title: Hydrocarbon concentration
frictionVectors.details: Dependence on offshore oil leaves fiscal stability exposed to price cycles and limits diversification. Foreign operators retain major roles in production, technology, and market access.

frictionVectors.title: Debt-linked infrastructure dependence
frictionVectors.details: Chinese financing and contractors remain important for roads, ports, and public works. Debt servicing and project opacity can narrow the government's room to negotiate sovereign control.

frictionVectors.title: Cocoa value-chain dependence
frictionVectors.details: Cote d'Ivoire remains a major cocoa producer but captures a limited share of downstream value. International buyers, sustainability rules, and price volatility constrain national control over the sector.

frictionVectors.title: External infrastructure influence
frictionVectors.details: French, Chinese, Gulf, and multilateral capital compete across ports, transport, and energy infrastructure. Diversification gives Abidjan leverage, but major projects still depend heavily on foreign finance and expertise.

highlights: Port and base diplomacy maximizes strategic rents

frictionVectors.title: Foreign military footprint
frictionVectors.details: U.S., Chinese, French, Japanese, and other military facilities provide revenue and strategic leverage but make Djibouti dependent on external security demand. Rivalry among these powers can constrain independent alignment.

frictionVectors.title: Port and debt concentration
frictionVectors.details: Djibouti's ports and trade corridors are central to its economy, yet external financing and creditor exposure limit policy flexibility. Competition over access to Ethiopian trade increases both bargaining power and vulnerability.

frictionVectors.title: Nile water security
frictionVectors.details: The GERD dispute with Ethiopia remains unresolved, leaving Egypt exposed to perceived risks over downstream water flows and regional bargaining power.

frictionVectors.title: External financing dependence
frictionVectors.details: IMF programs, Gulf investment, and foreign participation in major assets support stability but constrain Cairo's room to manage strategic infrastructure independently.

frictionVectors.title: Hydrocarbon dependency
frictionVectors.details: Falling oil output and limited economic diversification increase reliance on foreign operators, technology, and capital to sustain offshore production.

frictionVectors.title: Regional maritime competition
frictionVectors.details: Gulf of Guinea boundary and offshore-resource disputes require continued security and legal cooperation with neighboring states and external partners.

frictionVectors.title: Red Sea militarization
frictionVectors.details: Eritrea's coastline and proximity to the Bab el-Mandeb draw competing regional and extra-regional security interests, while tensions with Ethiopia remain a persistent risk.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign mining dependence
frictionVectors.details: Copper, zinc, and gold projects provide revenue but leave key extractive capacity dependent on foreign investors, contractors, and export infrastructure.

frictionVectors.title: External economic dependence
frictionVectors.details: Trade corridors, electricity, investment, and market access remain heavily tied to South Africa and the Southern African regional system.

frictionVectors.title: Fiscal and governance pressure
frictionVectors.details: Limited domestic revenue and political tensions increase reliance on external lenders, donors, and regional infrastructure networks.

frictionVectors.title: Nile diplomacy
frictionVectors.details: The GERD strengthens Ethiopia's energy and bargaining position, but unresolved relations with Egypt and Sudan keep water infrastructure politically sensitive.

frictionVectors.title: Debt and logistics exposure
frictionVectors.details: Debt restructuring, foreign-currency shortages, and dependence on external trade corridors limit Addis Ababa's control over major infrastructure and economic policy.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign Control of Extractives
frictionVectors.details: Oil and manganese remain heavily dependent on foreign operators and external capital. Libreville is seeking stronger state participation and better fiscal terms without disrupting production.

frictionVectors.title: Railway and Export Bottlenecks
frictionVectors.details: The Transgabon railway remains critical for manganese and timber exports, but aging infrastructure limits sovereign control over logistics and raises dependence on external financing.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign Fishing Pressure
frictionVectors.details: Industrial fishing by foreign fleets places pressure on coastal livelihoods and weakens oversight of maritime resources. Enforcement capacity remains limited.

frictionVectors.title: Energy and Port Dependence
frictionVectors.details: The Gambia relies on external partners for power generation, transport infrastructure, and major investment. Its geographic dependence on Senegal constrains independent infrastructure planning.

frictionVectors.title: Mining Sovereignty Gap
frictionVectors.details: Gold and emerging lithium projects attract substantial foreign capital while the state struggles to capture value and limit environmental damage. Illegal mining further undermines regulatory authority.

frictionVectors.title: Debt and Commodity Dependence
frictionVectors.details: IMF-linked fiscal reforms and dependence on gold, cocoa, and oil exports narrow policy space. External creditors and commodity-price volatility continue to influence national resource decisions.

frictionVectors.title: Simandou Foreign Consortiums
frictionVectors.details: The Simandou iron-ore complex is transforming Guinea's export prospects but remains dependent on Chinese-linked and other foreign consortiums for mines, rail, and port infrastructure.

frictionVectors.title: Bauxite Infrastructure Imbalance
frictionVectors.details: Bauxite revenues have not yet translated into broad domestic industrial capacity. Foreign operators control much of the logistics chain, while political uncertainty raises contract and sanctions risks.

frictionVectors.title: Cashew Export Dependence
frictionVectors.details: The economy remains heavily reliant on raw cashew exports, leaving farmers and state finances exposed to foreign buyers, price shocks, and weak domestic processing capacity.

frictionVectors.title: Fisheries and Port Influence
frictionVectors.details: Foreign fishing access and external involvement in port and maritime infrastructure limit effective control over coastal resources. Institutional fragility makes enforcement and transparent contracting difficult.

frictionVectors.title: External Debt and Project Conditionality
frictionVectors.details: IMF-linked fiscal reforms and major bilateral creditors constrain Nairobi's room to direct infrastructure and energy policy. Debt-service pressure increases leverage for external lenders over strategic assets and procurement.

frictionVectors.title: Lamu and Northern Corridor Competition
frictionVectors.details: Kenya is balancing Gulf, Chinese, Western, and regional interests around Lamu Port, transport corridors, and energy infrastructure. Insecurity and uneven commercial viability continue to limit full national control of these projects.

frictionVectors.title: Highlands Water Project Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Lesotho's water revenues and infrastructure are tightly tied to South African demand and financing. The arrangement provides essential income but leaves Maseru vulnerable to unequal bargaining power and project delays.

frictionVectors.title: Customs and Labor Reliance
frictionVectors.details: Dependence on South African markets, remittances, electricity links, and customs arrangements limits policy autonomy. Textile manufacturing also remains exposed to foreign buyers and shifting trade preferences.

frictionVectors.title: Iron Ore Concession Leverage
frictionVectors.details: Large-scale iron ore operations and associated rail and port infrastructure give foreign mining firms substantial influence over fiscal revenues and logistics. The government is seeking better local value capture while avoiding disruption to investment.

frictionVectors.title: Port and Corridor Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Monrovia's port and major transport corridors require external capital and technical support. Competing foreign commercial interests can narrow Liberia's ability to align infrastructure development with a broader national industrial strategy.

frictionVectors.title: Fragmented Oil Governance
frictionVectors.details: Rival political and security authorities continue to contest control over production, export terminals, and public spending. Foreign energy firms and intermediaries benefit from uncertainty while Libya struggles to convert oil wealth into sovereign development.

frictionVectors.title: Competing Foreign Military Influence
frictionVectors.details: Turkish, Russian, and other external security relationships remain embedded in Libya's divided political order. Military access and arms support affect control of ports, airbases, migration routes, and energy infrastructure.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign Control of Mining Value Chains
frictionVectors.details: Nickel, cobalt, graphite, and other mineral projects are dominated by foreign capital, technology, and export markets. Madagascar captures jobs and royalties but retains limited control over processing, pricing, and downstream value.

frictionVectors.title: Port, Power, and Food Vulnerability
frictionVectors.details: Unreliable electricity, weak transport links, and dependence on imported fuel and food increase exposure to external financiers and commodity shocks. Strategic mining and agricultural exports therefore do not reliably translate into broader sovereign resilience.

frictionVectors.title: Debt and aid conditionality
frictionVectors.details: External debt restructuring and IMF support constrain fiscal autonomy, while donor financing remains important for basic services and food security.

frictionVectors.title: Energy and mining dependence
frictionVectors.details: Power shortages and reliance on imported fuel weaken industrial sovereignty, even as uranium and rare-earth projects attract foreign capital.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign security dependence
frictionVectors.details: The junta has reduced Western military involvement while deepening ties with Russian security networks, creating new leverage risks despite its sovereignty-focused rhetoric.

frictionVectors.title: Mining control confrontation
frictionVectors.details: Efforts to increase state participation in gold mining are colliding with foreign operators, regulatory uncertainty, sanctions exposure, and persistent insecurity around production zones.

frictionVectors.title: GTA gas governance
frictionVectors.details: The shared Greater Tortue Ahmeyim project with Senegal offers major revenue potential but leaves Mauritania exposed to cross-border regulatory, fiscal, and operational disputes.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign-led extractive infrastructure
frictionVectors.details: Iron ore, green-hydrogen, and gas development rely heavily on external firms and finance, raising concerns over local value capture and strategic dependence.

frictionVectors.title: Chagos settlement implementation
frictionVectors.details: Mauritius is pursuing sovereignty over the Chagos Archipelago while managing the strategic and economic implications of the Diego Garcia military facility.

frictionVectors.title: External finance exposure
frictionVectors.details: The economy remains vulnerable to shifts in foreign investment, tourism, and offshore-finance rules, limiting policy autonomy despite strong institutions.

frictionVectors.title: Western Sahara resource diplomacy
frictionVectors.details: Phosphate, fisheries, and infrastructure projects in Western Sahara remain central to Morocco's sovereignty strategy and a recurring source of diplomatic and legal contestation.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign capital and water stress
frictionVectors.details: Automotive, renewable-energy, and port expansion strengthen industrial capacity but depend on external investors, while drought and water scarcity constrain long-term resource security.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign LNG Control
frictionVectors.details: Major offshore gas projects remain dominated by multinational operators and external financiers, limiting Mozambique's near-term control over revenues and infrastructure.

frictionVectors.title: Cabo Delgado Security Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Insurgent violence continues to constrain resource development, while Maputo relies heavily on regional and foreign security support to protect strategic assets.

frictionVectors.title: Offshore Oil Licensing
frictionVectors.details: New offshore discoveries are attracting international energy firms, creating pressure for stronger local participation, revenue safeguards, and environmental oversight.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign-Led Green Hydrogen
frictionVectors.details: Large external investments could accelerate industrialization but raise concerns over land, water, power infrastructure, and whether Namibia captures sufficient domestic value.

frictionVectors.title: Uranium and Mining Renegotiation
frictionVectors.details: The junta is seeking greater state control and better terms from foreign mining interests, but technical capacity, sanctions exposure, and investor flight constrain implementation.

frictionVectors.title: Benin Oil Corridor
frictionVectors.details: Export dependence on the Niger-Benin pipeline leaves oil revenues exposed to diplomatic disputes, border insecurity, and limited access to alternative transport routes.

frictionVectors.title: IOC and NNPC Bargaining
frictionVectors.details: Investment reforms aim to revive oil output, yet production sharing, divestments, and persistent crude theft continue to limit effective Nigerian control over the sector.

frictionVectors.title: Gas-to-Power Infrastructure Gap
frictionVectors.details: Pipeline constraints, payment arrears, and weak grid infrastructure prevent Nigeria from fully converting its gas resources into reliable domestic electricity and industrial growth.

frictionVectors.title: Conflict-Mineral Allegations
frictionVectors.details: Rwanda's mineral-trading position and alleged links to eastern Democratic Republic of the Congo supply chains attract diplomatic pressure and threaten access to premium markets.

frictionVectors.title: External Security Partnerships
frictionVectors.details: Rwanda's security relationships and overseas deployments expand its strategic leverage, but they also increase exposure to donor conditionality and regional backlash.

frictionVectors.title: Offshore Exploration Dependence
frictionVectors.details: São Tomé and Príncipe relies on foreign firms and licensing partners to assess offshore blocks, while commercial viability remains uncertain. Limited state capacity constrains bargaining power over future petroleum revenues.

frictionVectors.title: External Infrastructure Leverage
frictionVectors.details: Portugal, China, and other partners remain important for infrastructure, finance, and maritime security. The country seeks diversification without becoming dependent on any single external patron.

highlights: First oil and gas revenues are arriving

frictionVectors.title: Foreign Operator Renegotiation
frictionVectors.details: The government is pressing international oil and gas partners for improved fiscal terms and greater local participation while preserving production credibility. This creates tension with investors over contract stability and project economics.

frictionVectors.title: Fishing and Coastal Pressure
frictionVectors.details: Industrial and foreign fishing fleets face growing scrutiny amid concerns over depleted stocks, food security, and opaque licensing. Offshore petroleum development also raises risks for coastal livelihoods and maritime sovereignty.

highlights: Blue economy remains the core asset

frictionVectors.title: Maritime Security Competition
frictionVectors.details: Seychelles benefits from cooperation with India, France, the United States, and other partners on maritime surveillance and anti-piracy operations. Managing this assistance without appearing aligned against China remains a diplomatic constraint.

frictionVectors.title: Debt and Infrastructure Exposure
frictionVectors.details: Tourism dependence and climate vulnerability limit fiscal room for ports, energy, and resilience projects. External lenders and investors therefore retain substantial influence over strategic infrastructure choices.

highlights: Mining is driving a sovereignty test

frictionVectors.title: Foreign Mining Dominance
frictionVectors.details: Iron ore, rutile, and other mineral projects remain central to exports but are largely controlled or financed by foreign companies. The government faces pressure to increase local value addition, tax capture, and environmental accountability.

frictionVectors.title: Port and Power Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Freetown's port, transport corridors, and electricity system require sustained external capital and technical support. Dependence on overseas contractors and financiers can narrow the state's negotiating leverage over strategic infrastructure.

frictionVectors.title: Hydrocarbon Access Rivalry
frictionVectors.details: Foreign oil companies and external partners are pursuing Somali offshore opportunities while federal and regional authorities contest licensing and revenue-sharing powers. Weak institutions increase the risk that future resource wealth will deepen political fragmentation.

frictionVectors.title: Ports and Security Patronage
frictionVectors.details: Turkey, the Gulf states, the United States, and other actors compete for influence through military assistance, port access, and infrastructure partnerships. Al-Shabaab's insurgency and disputes between Mogadishu and federal member states limit effective national control.

frictionVectors.title: Strategic-Minerals Competition
frictionVectors.details: South Africa is balancing Chinese processing links, Western critical-minerals initiatives, and domestic beneficiation demands. Foreign capital remains important, but Pretoria retains substantial policy and regulatory leverage.

frictionVectors.title: Infrastructure Bottlenecks
frictionVectors.details: Electricity shortages, rail failures, and congestion at major ports weaken sovereign control over mineral exports. Mining firms and logistics partners are increasingly developing private infrastructure, creating parallel systems outside direct state capacity.

frictionVectors.title: Pipeline Dependence on Sudan
frictionVectors.details: South Sudan's oil exports depend on infrastructure crossing conflict-affected Sudan, leaving revenue and production vulnerable to external disruption. This dependence sharply limits Juba's bargaining autonomy.

frictionVectors.title: Armed Control of Resources
frictionVectors.details: Political and military elites continue to dominate oil revenues, transport corridors, and commercial concessions. Regional actors and foreign firms can secure access through elite networks rather than transparent national institutions.

frictionVectors.title: Externalized Gold Economy
frictionVectors.details: Gold production and smuggling networks help finance competing armed factions, with foreign traders and regional hubs capturing value outside formal state channels. The war has made resource sovereignty subordinate to battlefield financing.

frictionVectors.title: Port and Corridor Rivalry
frictionVectors.details: Control of Port Sudan and overland corridors has become strategically important to Gulf, Egyptian, Russian, and other external interests. Infrastructure access is increasingly tied to military influence and wartime bargaining.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign-Controlled Infrastructure
frictionVectors.details: Upgrades to Dar es Salaam port and regional rail corridors bring major Chinese, Gulf, and other foreign commercial interests into Tanzania's logistics sector. Dodoma is seeking stronger local-content and operating-control guarantees to prevent strategic dependence.

frictionVectors.title: Mining and LNG Negotiations
frictionVectors.details: Tanzania is pressing investors for greater state participation, processing, and revenue capture in minerals and offshore gas. Contract disputes and regulatory uncertainty remain the main friction points with foreign developers.

frictionVectors.title: Port Dependence and Foreign Finance
frictionVectors.details: Lomé's role as a gateway for landlocked Sahel states gives Togo strategic leverage, but port expansion and logistics depend heavily on foreign lenders, operators, and trading networks. This creates exposure to external commercial and security priorities.

frictionVectors.title: Northern Border Insecurity
frictionVectors.details: Militant activity and instability moving south from Burkina Faso threaten transport corridors and require expanding security cooperation with external partners. Counterterrorism needs may increase foreign influence over border infrastructure and intelligence systems.

frictionVectors.title: EU MIGRATION BARGAIN
frictionVectors.details: European funding and diplomatic pressure over irregular migration give Brussels substantial leverage over Tunisia's border and domestic policy choices.

frictionVectors.title: ENERGY IMPORT DEPENDENCE
frictionVectors.details: Declining domestic production and fiscal constraints leave Tunisia exposed to imported energy, while delayed infrastructure and financing limit near-term sovereign options.

frictionVectors.title: EACOP PRESSURE
frictionVectors.details: The Uganda-Tanzania oil pipeline remains strategically important but faces European political, legal, and financial opposition over climate and human-rights concerns.

frictionVectors.title: INFRASTRUCTURE DEBT EXPOSURE
frictionVectors.details: Chinese-backed transport and energy projects expand connectivity while increasing repayment obligations and reducing Kampala's room to maneuver.

frictionVectors.title: CRITICAL-MINERALS COMPETITION
frictionVectors.details: Western, Chinese, and Gulf investors are competing for copper and cobalt access, creating opportunities for Zambia but also pressure over ownership, processing, and export terms.

frictionVectors.title: POWER BOTTLENECK
frictionVectors.details: Hydropower shortages and drought-related generation losses constrain mining expansion and increase dependence on regional electricity imports and emergency infrastructure.

frictionVectors.title: MINERAL PROCESSING CONTROL
frictionVectors.details: Harare is tightening controls on lithium and other strategic minerals, but foreign capital and technology remain essential, limiting effective domestic control over value chains.

frictionVectors.title: SANCTIONS AND FINANCIAL ISOLATION
frictionVectors.details: Sanctions, restricted access to international finance, and currency instability push Zimbabwe toward opaque bilateral arrangements and deepen reliance on non-Western partners.
